intro: Racing strings give a march room to grow, from a quiet clarinet tune to a G-major finish with bass drum and cymbals. Tchaikovsky puts this apparently conclusive celebration one movement before the symphony’s slow lament.

sections.label: A · Racing strings, quick woodwinds
sections.mNote: Strings run in groups of three beneath wind replies

sections.label: B · The clarinets’ E-major march
sections.mNote: Clarinets give the march its first complete statement

sections.label: A′ · The racing strings return
sections.mNote: The opening scherzo resumes after the march

sections.label: Link · Gathering over D
sections.mNote: A held D prepares the march’s return in G

sections.label: B′ · G major with drums
sections.mNote: The march returns with bass drum and cymbals

sections.label: Coda · Scales plunge towards G
sections.mNote: Strings and low brass descend into the final G-major chords

cues.title: Strings on the run
cues.text: The strings race in groups of three, with quick woodwind replies above them. A march begins to appear among the running notes, little scraps of a tune that will eventually command the whole orchestra.
cues.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 15: opening strings, winds and emerging march fragments. https://qso.com.au/uploads/QSO-Learning-Resource-Breathtaking-Tchaikovsky-1-.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Clarinets claim the march
cues.text: The clarinets play the march in full, quietly and in E major, while the strings keep moving underneath. The tune acquires its boots before it acquires its drums.
cues.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 15, reproduces the clarinet theme. E-major key and quiet unison scoring: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Back to the quick strings
cues.text: The opening scherzo returns. Running string figures and woodwind scales resume their exchanges, with the complete march now lodged in the memory.
cues.evidence: Third-movement recapitulation described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky); Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 15.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: D holds the door
cues.text: The preparation rests on D, the dominant of G major. The orchestra gathers around that held note before the march returns in the movement’s home key.
cues.evidence: Tchaikovsky’s third-movement sketch specifies a reprise of the scherzo with a pedal on D before the G-major march. Quoted in the composition history: https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Symphony_No._6.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The march gets its drums
cues.text: The march returns in G major, now with bass drum and cymbals. The same tune that first belonged to quiet clarinets fills the orchestra.
cues.evidence: Third-movement G-major march and percussion scoring: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky); Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 15.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: An ending planned first
cues.text: In his February 1893 sketches, Tchaikovsky reminds himself that the first job after returning from a trip is to compose this ending. He wants the G-major march “in a solemnly triumphant manner”.
cues.evidence: Tchaikovsky’s inscription in the third-movement sketches, 11 February 1893 Old Style (23 February New Style), quoted at https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Symphony_No._6.

cues.title: Four octaves down
cues.text: The ending sends scales plunging through four octaves in the violins and then the low brass. They land on G major with the force of a finale. One movement remains: Adagio lamentoso.
cues.evidence: Harlow Robinson’s Boston Symphony programme note describes the four-octave descent and G-major landing. https://www.bso.org/works/tchaikovsky-symphony-no-6
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The clarinets finish the tune
transitions.how: Fragments of the march collect into a complete E-major tune for unison clarinets. The strings continue their running accompaniment beneath its longer notes. The march emerges quietly from music already in motion.
transitions.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 15; E-major clarinet scoring: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky).

transitions.title: Two bars back to the scherzo
transitions.how: A two-bar link takes the march back to the opening scherzo. The strings recover their quick groups of three, and wind replies break across them. Tchaikovsky moves straight into the return without a separate development section.
transitions.evidence: Third-movement exposition-to-recapitulation link: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky). Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 15, describes the returning scherzo.

transitions.title: The bass holds D
transitions.how: The returning scherzo reaches a pedal on D. Holding this dominant beneath the continuing figures prepares G major, the key of the march’s final statement.
transitions.evidence: The composer’s third-movement sketch explicitly links the scherzo reprise, a pedal on D and the final G-major march. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Symphony_No._6

transitions.title: From D to the G-major march
transitions.how: The D pedal leads to the march in G major. Strings and winds broaden the tune, and bass drum and cymbals join the returning march. Its first quiet clarinet statement now has a full orchestral answer.
transitions.evidence: Pedal and G-major destination: https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Symphony_No._6. The final march’s scoring is described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky).

transitions.title: Scales drive into the final chords
transitions.how: The march’s closing phrases send descending scales through the violins and then the trombones and tuba. Their four-octave plunge lands on G major; brass and percussion reinforce the final chords.
transitions.evidence: Harlow Robinson, Boston Symphony programme note on Symphony No. 6, third-movement ending. https://www.bso.org/works/tchaikovsky-symphony-no-6

source.title: Tchaikovsky, Symphony No. 6, III, historical full-score scan
source.locator: PDF p. 1 running strings; march and return across the movement; final pages show full orchestral cadence. Entries describe passage-level roles, not continuous instrumentation.

timeline.note: Opening region: fast violin figures are joined by wind replies; lower strings articulate the foundation.
Early orchestral build: piccolo, brass and timpani join the running strings (score PDF pp. 12–13). The report’s 1:22 boundary anchors the broad stronger passage before the lighter march.
First march region: a firmer melodic profile emerges against the still-mobile orchestral surface.
First-march expansion: trumpet and bass-trombone phrases reinforce winds, horns and strings (score PDF p. 20). The report’s 2:38 change supplies an approximate passage anchor.
The first-march close adds piccolo to upper winds and trumpet punctuation (score PDF p. 22), then reduces into the scherzo return. The 3:40 report boundary anchors the region.
Scherzo return: quick string figures and wind exchanges recover the opening texture.
Preparation: reduced orchestral texture builds through repeated figures and a sustained foundation.
Later march region: strings, winds and brass accumulate, with percussion reinforcing the stronger statements.
Closing drive: brass, percussion and strings reinforce the emphatic G-major ending.

composer.epithet: He could make a ballroom glitter, then let one unguarded melody tell us who was unhappy there.
facts: School of Jurisprudence; Saint Petersburg Conservatory, 1862–65, with Anton Rubinstein and Nikolai Zaremba
Nadezhda von Meck: an allowance, 1877–90, and a friendship conducted by letter
Three ballets; Eugene Onegin, The Queen of Spades and other operas
composer.background:
At Kamenka on 6 July 1878, Tchaikovsky was explaining to Nadezhda von Meck how he composed. Ideas arrived in the middle of conversations; he held them in his head until he could sketch them on the first sheet of paper that came to hand. Waiting for the right mood was no way to work. “Inspiration is a guest who does not like to visit the idle,” he told her. Then he broke off for dinner. At two o’clock he resumed, moving on to sketching, orchestration, fair copies and how far a symphony must keep to its traditional form. Here is the composer of extravagant passions in his own voice: observant, companionable, exact about his trade.

He was born in Votkinsk, where his father managed an ironworks. He grew deeply attached to his French governess, Fanny Dürbach, and began piano lessons at the end of 1845. The profession chosen for him was the law. In 1850 he entered the preparatory class of the Imperial School of Jurisprudence in Saint Petersburg. Four years later his mother died of cholera. He graduated in 1859 and took a post at the Ministry of Justice, while opera and concerts increasingly claimed his attention.
